📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 1936, Federico García Lorca, the Spanish poet and playwright, was working on a new play, La Bola Negra, which was never completed. Only four pages of it were found. Later that year, the 38-year-old homosexual anti-fascist sympathizer was executed during the Spanish Civil War on the orders of right-wing military authorities. Ninety years later, Spanish directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi have crafted a new, ambitious film named after these scant remnants. Their glamorous but gritty film stars Spaniards Miguel Bernardeau, of Elite fame, along with Álvaro Lafuente Calvo, the singer known as Guitarricadelafuente, in his first major acting role. La Bola Negra is an epic that spans close to a century; it follows several gay men whose lives are bound together by their identities, love and loss, and the looming presence of the Spanish Civil War, all under the shadow of García Lorca’s work.

Sources indicate that there are works of art that escape definitions, pieces of media that transcend. La Bola Negra, both the film and the play, is a biography and a document of war; a love story and a tale of generational trauma; an examination of queerness in Spanish history. The film contains stories that speak of fear, of desire, of guilt, and of shame. And it is a work that defies the easy summary of a logline.

In a recent development, “So you would like us to craft that sentence for you,” Bernardeau, 29, notes, laughing while sitting next to Guitarricadelafuente at a restaurant in Manhattan. He’s athletic and handsome. He comes across as a classic macho onscreen, perhaps a residue of the characters he’s been cast as, but in person he is softer and warm, thoughtful. His hair is cut in a shaggy semi-mullet, and he’s wearing a Dolce & Gabbana black T-shirt featuring a young Monica Bellucci, a vintage find.

“It’s a movie that when you finish it, it makes you want to live,” Guitarricadelafuente, 29, claims. His curly hair spills over his forehead onto his wire-frame eyeglasses. As Guitarrica—a diminutive for guitar in Aragonese (his family has roots in Aragon) and his stage-name shorthand—he sings about romance and sex, mixing the sounds of Spanish tradition with the synths and reverberations of pop. Like Bernardeau, he’s disarmingly attractive, but his persona is more open. Not unlike their characters, Bernardeau appears more stoic, as if he’s standing on firmer ground; Guitarrica is lighter on his feet and bashful, perhaps settling into the newness of being a movie star.

“Not to be dramatic,” Guitarrica continues, “but people, friends that have seen the movie with us, it takes them a moment to compose themselves after,” he notes. “Like, fuck, it’s an intense film. I think it makes you want to live and not do anything half-hearted.” Bernardeau looks at his costar with admiration and utters a line from the film: “Nadie desaparece del todo” (No one disappears completely). “It’s a phrase that Rafael says that keeps coming back to me,” he says.

In a recent development, with the enormity of approaching García Lorca, an idol for Spaniards, a paragon for writers, and a hero for queer men, Calvo and Ambrossi (both modern versions of all these things) were not bold enough to attempt to complete La Bola Negra. Instead they built an affecting universe around it, drawing inspiration from it and other works by García Lorca, as well as co-writer Alberto Conejero’s La Piedra Oscura. The latter was itself loosely inspired by Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, a companion of García Lorca and a member of his theater troupe, who died as a soldier during the civil war.

It has been revealed that the film tells three stories: that of Sebastián (Guitarrica) in 1937, a young trumpeter taken into the Nationalist army who encounters Rafael (Bernardeau) as a new prisoner put under his watch; of Carlos (Milo Quifes) in 1932, the lead character in García Lorca’s original play and a young gay man who is denied membership to a casino club because of his sexuality; and in 2017, of Alberto (Carlos González), a modern-day historian who, following the death of his grandfather and an excavation into his past, finds himself indelibly connected to the other men. In Carlos’s vignette, club members vote on his admission using black and white balls, where a black ball (la bola negra) signifies a negative. When Carlos receives several, he has to confront his father. The tension between shame and confession becomes the heart of the film.

In a recent development, sebastián is a character who is, as Guitarrica puts it, “like a custom-made suit” for him. He ran into Ambrossi and Calvo after performing at the Primavera Sound festival in Barcelona two years ago. “It was one of those nights where, after a few drinks, you kind of forget what was noted,” he says with a laugh. But he heard from Calvo after that, and soon he was in Madrid meeting with the directors. “I thought they’d ask me to make a song for the soundtrack,” he says. Instead they told him they were writing a film with Conejero, and offered him the role of Sebastián. “I wasn’t confident at all, nothing was clear,” Guitarrica says, “but I saw the faith they had in me.”.

Recent findings suggest that bernardeau, who was invited to audition for Rafael, also had his doubts. “I didn’t think I did well,” Bernardeau states of his audition. “I was like damn, I missed the opportunity of a lifetime.” But after a week and a half of self-inflicted torture, he was asked to read with Guitarrica and was then offered the role. He was sure about his costar: “The choice of Álvaro made perfect sense,” he says.

Bernardeau and Guitarrica were familiar with each other’s work. “But we met as Sebastián and Rafael,” Bernardeau says. These days they appear to have the kind of friendship, of reverence for each other, of two men who’ve gone to war together—even if just on camera.

In a recent development, despite its hefty emotional punch and astonishing staging, La Bola Negra is a film about war. Human stories are its spoils, and the unrealized potential of lost lives is buried on the battlefields. The Spanish Civil War still looms darkly over the country. Their dead, from unknown soldiers to acclaimed names like García Lorca, have become Spain’s ghosts.

Recent findings suggest that “I felt a ton of responsibility,” Bernardeau says of playing Rafael, with his connection to a real person. “There is a responsibility in telling the story of someone who is no longer here,” he says. “By making this film, I found that he is crucial to many people, and I didn’t know that.” Bernardeau knew of García Lorca much like anyone who learns about their home country’s foremost literary giants in school, but the life of Rafael perhaps eluded the textbooks. (Ambrossi and Calvo gave him a reading list, and Bernardeau got to work.).

Industry observers note that for Guitarrica, the process was more internal. The character of Sebastián was crafted for him, which afforded him the license to find himself in the role, he indicates, and consider history by imagining what it would have been like to have lived it.

It has been revealed that “There was a lot of introspection,” he notes. Guitarrica was also learning how to arrive at certain emotions “and unearth my own experiences to be able to give nuance to my character,” he says. Back in Madrid, during that first meeting with the directors, they asked him if he had any emotional traumas. “I said no, and they said, we’ll see,” he says, laughing. Acting, Guitarrica has found, means excavating old wounds. Did he encounter any turmoil? “Well, yes,” he laughs, “but I’m not telling you about that.”.

It has been revealed that since the film premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May and received a 20-minute standing ovation, with Ambrossi and Calvo winning the award for best direction (alongside Fatherland director Pawel Pawlikowski), Bernardeau and Guitarrica have covered magazines in Spain and beyond and become two of the internet’s latest fixations. La Bola Negra will also represent Spain in the best international feature film category at the Academy Awards, should it be nominated.

“I love that it’s a story that we feel is so ours, that is such a fundamental part of our society and our collective imagination,” Bernardeau states. “The war has impacted us through generations, and it is part of us in different ways.”.

Industry observers note that he notes he doesn’t want to romanticize, but the global reception of such a regional story has given him some faith in humanity. “Because, in the end, it indicates that we’re all different, but all the same; that the most personal is also the most creative,” he says, making sure I know that he’s quoting a phrase attributed to Martin Scorsese.

In a recent development, “I think that this film is largely about an idea that is pretty straightforward,” Guitarrica states. “Simply, it’s about the drive to live. Of not leaving anything on the table or unfinished. And that is a very universal story.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bowen Yang made a surprise cameo on Saturday Night Live this past weekend.
  • In a recent development, yang is at the moment crushing it as Mary Todd Lincoln in the Broadway production of Oh, Mary!
  • According to recent reports, it’s unclear exactly when the details of Yang’s appearance came together, but he reportedly did head to Studio 8H after his Broadway show on Friday to do a rehearsal for his two scenes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bowen Yang made a surprise cameo on Saturday Night Live this past weekend. The beloved former cast member appeared in multiple sketches, first as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the cold open and later as Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel in John Mulaney’s wild musical number about Latest York City. Yang seemed comfortable and back in his element, but it turns out the behind the scenes wasn’t exactly smooth sailing. Sarah Sherman actually had to fill in for him during dress rehearsal, leading to a hilarious visual that’s making the rounds.

In a recent development, yang is at the moment crushing it as Mary Todd Lincoln in the Broadway production of Oh, Mary! His schedule on the show, however, isn’t exactly SNL friendly. The Lyceum Theatre offers two performances every Saturday: one at 5 PM and one at 8:30 PM. Since SNL’s dress rehearsal starts at 8 PM, there was no way for the actor to appear in both; so, during the cold open, Sarah Sherman appeared in Yang’s part, hilariously wearing a sign that mentioned Bowen Yang. According to Late Nighter, Marcello Hernández warned the crowd ahead of time, though I can’t imagine they expected this visual, which Yang later posted to his Instagram account….

A post shared by Bowen Yang (@fayedunaway).

According to recent reports, it’s unclear exactly when the details of Yang’s appearance came together, but he reportedly did head to Studio 8H after his Broadway show on Friday to do a rehearsal for his two scenes. I can’t imagine longtime showrunner Lorne Michaels would be okay with a random celebrity doing a cameo without the standard rehearsing schedule, but he obviously knows Bowen well enough to know he didn’t need the full runthrough.

He clearly didn’t either, as he was a standout during the live show in both the cold open and as Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel in the musical number. Saidah Belo-Osagie reportedly played the second part very capably during the dress rehearsal, but that was never going to work for the live show. She had another role in the sketch, and also, Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel was clearly written for Yang, as he’s currently playing Mary Todd Lincoln in the aforementioned show. He probably would have been personally offended if he wasn’t asked and tuned into SNL to see someone else doing an outrageous take on the part he’s currently playing on Broadway.

It has been revealed that we’ve gotten two consecutive weeks with cameos from former cast members, as Bobby Moynihan appeared in the Davis S Pumpkins anniversary sketch and in a segment on Weekend Enhancement as Drunk Uncle. Personally, I’d love to see SNL try and do double appearances more often. It’s always fun to see old favorites surprise fans by appearing in a sketch, but it’s even more fun to see those familiar faces show up twice during the same episode so they have a little more to do.

SNL is currently on hiatus for a few weeks, but it’ll return in early December with a newly introduced episode hosted by Amanda Seyfried. I cannot wait, as she should bring something new and exciting to 30 Rock and will hopefully continue the momentum as the show has recently dropped its strongest episodes of the season, including this past weekend's heater where John Mulaney brought some of the sharpest social commentary we've gotten in a long time.

#16731. Breaking: My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2080 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east.
  • I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less.
  • According to recent reports, it should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east. Yet, I still can’t reach out and grasp the throne that sits right in front of me. I’m Marco Sanudo, and the throne of the serene republic of Venice eludes me.

I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less. I’ve managed to avoid punishment for that crime, despite the fact it earned me a fiefdom to rule while I’ve tried to up my patrician score enough to be the lucky party the next time a ruling Doge dies in office (or runs out their 10 year term). Sadly, Doge Leonardo, the mysterious masked lord who’s had an iron grip on power since the first couple of old blokes to hold the position in this playthrough popped their clogs, is proving incredibly tough to oust.

According to recent reports, it should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast. It certainly did in being granted a pardon for offing that other Marco, but not even that and a plague which infected nearly everyone in the realm aside from me have paved the way to Dogedom. In the meantime, I’ve striven to gain wealth and influence. I’ve worked up to having four trade routes running at once, with goods like wine, iron, and textiles flowing from market to market across southern Europe and bringing a steady supply of coin back to my Venetian estate. I’ve built trade posts at the extremities of my routes, giving me the option of starting from further afield and reaching newly introduced lands if the cash flow dries up closer to home.

This is where Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion has blended a bit with the game’s traditional feudal moneymaking to supercharge my coffers. The land holding I killed a dude for, the Proveditorate of Zara, means I’ve also had tax money from modern day Croatia to add to both my trade profits and the income my domicile generates on its own. I am, as the medieval kids say, minted.

In a recent development, getting to the point of serious pocket clinkage is, as you might imagine given Silk and Silver’s focus on filling the game’s world with travelling merchant companies and wheeler-dealing republican patrician families, the beating heart of the expansion. A near-constant stream of notifications about prices of different goods I’m trying to hawk in different locations encourage me to regularly prune and re-work my routes so that max profits are being earned and no carrying capacity’s being wasted. The bubbling up of wars and plagues impacts prices in affected cities, making it a never-ending battle if you’re desperate to optimise everything within an inch of its life. I’ve found that degree of micromanagement unnecessary if the goal is just to keep a decent profit margin ticking over. Just remember to replace the trader assigned to a route if they die, recall them every few years so they don’t stress themselves to death, and check in every so often to re-evaluate whether you’re running goods that are suitably in demand.

Sources indicate that if you stick at it for a decent amount of time, with a certain type of good - alcohol or jewellery, for example - your expertise in dealing in them increases, making it easier to sell for better prices. Trade routes left running between the same markets also gain boons from being in place for a long time, offering a counterpoint to rejigging them every five seconds to wring out a few more coins. Most of my routes have run along a path that includes stops at four markets, with the occasional location boasting a monopoly I’ve bargained for with the local ruler, so I don’t have to worry about competition at every stop.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re playing as a merchant who isn’t locked into the ruling inner circle of a republic, making your routes as lengthy as possible is one of the three moneymaking areas your firm can specialise in. That first one’s caravaneering, and is the one I leant into in a non-Marco Sanudo playthrough. Beyond that, you can become an expert loan shark, lending cash to rulers or paying their ransoms in order to recoup interest and collect hooks you can use for favours. Manufacturing expensive artifacts that can be sold individually to collectors for a profit is the third option. The latter two I’ve only dabbled in a little bit as of writing, having earned enough gold mostly from caravanneering to buy the land containing the city with my home market and be anointed a Sheikh. So, beginning as a landless merchant is a nice alternative to Crusader Kings 3’s long-established wandering adventurer starting point, with both allowing you to work your way up from lowly serf to landed lordly dynasty in your location of choice.

If you’re after a more specific historical scenario, Silk and Silver has Guelphs and Ghibellines. This is where we find Marco Sanudo, as well as the other patrician family head I’ve played as thus far, Speronella Dalesmanni. The setup is that the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor have had a bit of a tiff, essentially rooted in who should have certain powers, with different cities and powerful families in northern Italy taking either the Guelph (Pope-likers) or Ghibelline (Holy Roman Empire-enjoyers) side depending on what suits their goals or principles. I’ll be honest, aside from being another way to easily earn friends or enemies in the ruthless crucible of merchant republican politics, where votes and reputation-bolstering aid from other nobles are key, the situation’s not had a hugely obvious bearing on my playthroughs thus far.

Sources indicate that I think the closest it’s come is during my Dalesmanni run, if largely due to the existence of the By God Alone expansion allowing a latest branch of Catholicism, dubbed Italian Christianity, to be created. The initial conversion push from the bishop responsible led a number of my fellow northern Italian nobles away from the Roman Rite headed by his Popeliness, making the Guelph/Ghibelline split more clearly defined.

Sources indicate that in the early hours of both my Sanudo and Dalesmanni playthroughs, I’ve been far more focused on simply trying to push the respective patrician families up the hill from posh toffs with naught but a vote and a manor to elected rulers of their great cities, with land holdings to match. Speronella’s situation in Padua is made incredibly tough by the fact she’s a woman in a world where every succession rule is designed to put blokes first, so I’ve had more success with Marco and his quest to become the Doge of Venice.

As the head of a patrician family, one of select few elite clans who steer the oligarchical republic, I was faced with earning Marco enough respect among his fellow family heads that they’d consider voting him to the top of the succession list, thus securing his power whenever the current Doge got the boot. Pulling that off, while also not kowtowing to the requests and schemes of those same peers, isn’t easy. A large cocktail of factors go into determining whether another noble likes you enough to vote in support of your succession. There’s your patrician rating, which is upped by doing things which specifically show you to be good at this Italian noble house lark, such as establishing trade monopolies for the republic, gaining the Pope’s favour, or having close relatives who also hold key positions in the republic. However, how close a friendship you have with the target and how their character traits align with you also play a huge rule.

Industry observers note that thus it was that, at one point, Marco was best mates with the current Doge and had a decent patrician rating, but had only amassed 68 of the 72 points needed for mentioned Doge to vote for him because the Doge was generous, and therefore didn’t care for Marco’s ambitiousness. That same Doge either liked or respected Marco enough to grant him a council position and the status of regent, but he would not back Marco to replace him permanently for love nor money. This is the same man who liked Marco so much that when I pulled off that not-so-sneaky murder on another noble house head in order to inherit the keys to the Proveditorate of Zara, the Doge was instantly willing to pardon me and prevent Marco suffering any punishment for the crime.

Not even a couple of serious plagues hitting Venice, which at one point had all three people ahead of Marco in the queue suffering from smallpox, could get him on that throne. Eventually, it took a bit of lucky timing when his Doge mate died of old age - a few years after beating smallpox - to finally install Marco as Doge. Given that delayed promotion, as of writing I’ve not yet had enough time in the substantial chair to give a proper verdict on how it differs from regular feudal rulerdom in the long run.

It has been revealed that what I can do instead is tell you a bit about the fun of council votes. The same pool of voters who in a republic like Venice, get a say in who succeeds the ruler, also vote on the passage of laws and decrees. One proposal you can put forward is a vote to change who exactly is allowed a seat in this voting pool. It defaults to just being heads of patrician families, but can be extended to include all vassals, or tightened up so only the Doge’s councillors or the ruler themselves have a say, that being the way despotism lies. As you can imagine, passing a change to who can vote can drastically change the state of play, either tightening up the number of folks who might oppose or support you, or bringing new folks into play in a fashion that dilutes individual power, but gives you more pieces on the board to mind or manipulate to your advantage.

I’ve found it suitably tough to orchestrate successful votes to change laws and customs which medieval Italian noble families, expectedly, have firmly entrenched stances on. Getting rid of checks and balances, such as the requirement to vote on banishments or wars - so the Doge can rule as a despot - has proven one such challenge, as has changing laws governing men being prioritised over women. I tried to pass equal succession as a substitute for men being put first while playing as Speronella, but met an insurmountable wall of resistance due to the region’s culture and faith. So, all I could do was try to put my young male heir in the best position possible to make the sorts of gains I couldn’t.

Much easier to weasel into place, either through some canny swaying or the offering of hooks, are laws giving state backing or other priority to trading in certain types of goods. Alcohol, for instance, which certainly hasn’t hurt the profits of Marco’s two wine trade routes.

Thus, cash continues to flow through the tentacles of my trade empire in sizable globs. As he’s now Doge, I’ve got Marco using the ample funds of Venice’s treasury to build a new piazza and have him focused on making the city’s already-strong trade league even more formidable, by attracting new members from the few other northern Italian blocs.

While I’m fairly sure there are folks who’ll find Silk and Silver's constant barrage of trade route notifications annoying, or that their power-grabbing skills and sheer multitude of money-making means combine to make playthroughs less challenging than they could be, so far I've found it another enjoyably sonorous string to Crusader Kings 3’s bow. Above all else, playing as a merchant gives more reason to invest in stewardship skills beyond just maximising your tax yields, while the republican politics of the DLC's main region fleshes out rewarding intrigue-focused builds. Diplomacy and martial skills are less key, but still have their place at times.

If you’re an absolute stickler for historical accuracy, you may well find other things to gripe about, but aside from the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict fading into the background, I’ve found plenty to like in my quest to become top Doge.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that you probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking.
  • In a recent development, as reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device.
  • There are two silver linings here, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

In a recent development, as reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It right now affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for customers to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to matter these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

Recent findings suggest that this flaw is perhaps the most notable to fix, but it's not the only serious concern. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this matter. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Legend of Zelda was in "dire straits" before Breath of the Wild gave the beloved series a massive second wind, according to two former Nintendo marketing leads.
  • In a recent development, the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most recent remake has been a mega success, becoming the fastest-selling Switch 2 game so far, but the shiny new adventure has also prompted some online debate over where the series should go next.
  • Nintendo of America's ex-director of social media marketing Kit Ellis and former public relations manager Krysta Yang chimed in on the discourse in their latest podcast (below), and explained that Zelda wasn't doing too hot before the Switch era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Legend of Zelda was in "dire straits" before Breath of the Wild gave the beloved series a massive second wind, according to two former Nintendo marketing leads.

In a recent development, the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most recent remake has been a mega success, becoming the fastest-selling Switch 2 game so far, but the shiny new adventure has also prompted some online debate over where the series should go next. Should Zelda lean into its carefully directed history - like the one brilliantly remade in Ocarina of Time - or keep the ball rolling with Breath of the Wild's wide open, spontaneous sandbox?

Nintendo of America's ex-director of social media marketing Kit Ellis and former public relations manager Krysta Yang chimed in on the discourse in their latest podcast (below), and explained that Zelda wasn't doing too hot before the Switch era.

"There has been some revisionist history out there lately," Ellis said in response to fans who reckon "the Zelda team ripped away" series staples, like classic dungeons and linear worlds, at the height of their popularity.

According to recent reports, "I remember, I was going to the focus groups where it was a really dark moment," Ellis continued. "The feedback was like, 'The fan base is dwindling. This is not bringing in new players.'".

The Legend of Zelda was supposedly "shrinking," while "interest in the audience was getting smaller and smaller" with each new entry. "They had to do something dramatic," Ellis said.

It has been revealed that "This series was in dire straits. They were selling, like, nothing," Yang added.

The Zelda series was certainly never irrelevant, but there's a pretty big gap between the roughly 8m copies Twilight Princess sold at the beginning of the Wii generation, the roughly 3m copies Skyward Sword sold at the end of the console's life, and the 34m copies that Breath of the Wild sold just one console generation later.

Sources indicate that it was a success so big it spawned a wildly ambitious sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, and even influenced the latest 2D Zelda, Echoes of Wisdom. Now that classic Zelda's back in the spotlight, though, I do hope Nintendo's able to slot the series' curated dungeons into whatever the next mainline game becomes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6 isn't even out yet, but it's been estimated that Rockstar's next game has already surpassed $1.45 billion in revenue, with almost 15 million copies sold via pre-orders.
  • That's according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, whose latest sales tracker estimates – updated yesterday – continue to put PS5 pre-orders well ahead of Xbox Series X|S, with sales for Sony's console thought to account for 74% of the lot, at 11.13 million copies.
  • According to recent reports, what's more, as of November 10, Sensor Tower estimated that a whopping 87% of all GTA 6 pre-orders were for the more expensive Ultimate Edition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 isn't even out yet, but it's been estimated that Rockstar's next game has already surpassed $1.45 billion in revenue, with almost 15 million copies sold via pre-orders.

That's according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, whose latest sales tracker estimates – updated yesterday – continue to put PS5 pre-orders well ahead of Xbox Series X|S, with sales for Sony's console thought to account for 74% of the lot, at 11.13 million copies. Between both platforms, Sensor Tower estimates 14.94 million units have been sold.

According to recent reports, what's more, as of November 10, Sensor Tower estimated that a whopping 87% of all GTA 6 pre-orders were for the more expensive Ultimate Edition. As a reminder of the different GTA 6 versions, the Standard Edition is $80, while the Ultimate Edition comes in at $100, the price everyone was so worried about before pre-orders were announced. For your extra $20, you get some unique cars and several exclusive shops, among other things – I imagine those shops may have been the selling point for many, given that you're literally missing out on content otherwise.

To an extent, I'd imagine a bit of a 'go big or go home' mindset might apply here, too. After all, we've been waiting 13 years since the last game in the series, so a lot of people are just going to want the, well, ultimate experience. It's this sort of thinking that could get you to spend $400 on a box of mostly expensive tat, though, so be careful with that.

It has been revealed that anyway, there was never any doubt GTA 6 sales would be massive, but it'll be interesting to see exactly where they land at and after launch. Sony and Microsoft have already unveiled that it's the most pre-ordered game of all time on their respective digital storefronts, and there are still a couple of days to go until release. According to Sensor Tower, though, the biggest spike in pre-orders came right after the release of Netflix's Extended Look – sales rose 6x compared to the previous tracked day, with August 28 (the day after the premiere) thought to have brought in around $16.3 million in revenue. So, it sounds like most people were already sold once they got a proper look at the gameplay footage.

GTA 6 preloads are already live, so if you've pre-ordered the digital version – or the code-in-a-box release, if you have yours – you can start getting it downloaded now so you're ready for launch on November 19.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, newly introduced multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five.
  • Sources indicate that deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities.
  • There's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, newly introduced multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Sources indicate that deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

There's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

It has been revealed that spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

It has been revealed that you can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

Recent findings suggest that as has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

It's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

Final Fantasy 14's ongoing pursuit in making its 500-hour story less daunting almost manifested into something in August, but Yoshi-P decided to postpone it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I can also recognise that for anyone trying to start the game in the big 2026, it's incredibly daunting.
  • We know, at the very least, that director and producer Naoki Yoshida has been thinking about ways to make that barrier to entry a little less frightening—he mentioned as much during Final Fantasy 14's Berlin Fan Festival—but according to a recent Letter from the Producer, it turns out we could've actually had something as recently as August.
  • "The idea of letting players freely choose a starting point for their adventure has been discussed, with the goal being to offer players a range of choices, rather than prescribe their experience according to my philosophy," Yoshida wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love Final Fantasy 14. I can also recognise that for anyone trying to start the game in the big 2026, it's incredibly daunting. Being faced with A Realm Reborn and five entire expansions' worth of story is a lot, and the question of how to funnel newly introduced players into Eorzea in a more approachable manner while still respecting the MMO's heavily narrative-driven vibe has been an ongoing debate for the last several years.

We know, at the very least, that director and producer Naoki Yoshida has been thinking about ways to make that barrier to entry a little less frightening—he mentioned as much during Final Fantasy 14's Berlin Fan Festival—but according to a recent Letter from the Producer, it turns out we could've actually had something as recently as August.

"The idea of letting players freely choose a starting point for their adventure has been discussed, with the goal being to offer players a range of choices, rather than prescribe their experience according to my philosophy," Yoshida wrote.

In case you're not familiar with Yoshida's whole stance on this, he's long been staunchly protective of Final Fantasy 14's narrative integrity. Story skips are locked to the cash shop and, up until now, never included the current expansion. He's repeatedly expressed the fact that he's not too keen on letting people jump in wherever they feel, since it kinda mucks up the decade-plus worldbuilding and character relationships the game has built.

But, like many things he's been opposed to introducing in the game like unlocked glamour, he's letting up for the sake of allowing players more agency in how they engage with the game.

Anyway, back to letting people tackle its immense story a little easier. "With New Game+ working smoothly, this approach could work," Yoshida surmised. "In fact, we'd been laying groundwork to make this a possibility in conjunction with the release of the Nintendo Switch 2 version, but ultimately decided to postpone this initiative.".

In a recent development, I do wonder specifically what made them stop—whether there was a hiccup somewhere, or whether Yoshida simply decided now wasn't the right time. He also expresses concern about a mismatch in player skill between those who jump ahead and those who've been around the block. "Even if you could start adventuring from a point of your choosing, the time and effort required to master a job remain a constant," he wrote. "We also need to avoid situations where both upcoming and veteran players are left confused when matched together.".

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

In a recent development, I don't want to be the one to tell Yoshi-P that the mismatch is still there even among players who've been around a long time, but I've seen an awful lot of omni-level characters who can't even do their basic rotation. So there's that.

"However, with all these considerations in mind, we've held meetings to discuss system and tutorial improvements, and have set ourselves a significant goal for the future. Although we'll need more time to realise this goal, I think giving players more freedom in their adventures will ultimately prove a positive change.".

Honestly? I think even without story skips, tutorialisation and job mastery need to be better woven into the fabric of the game. Its low-level Hall of the Novice misses crucial info and includes odd holdovers from the days of things like the TP resource and much tougher aggro management—there's no emphasis on the importance of healers dealing damage, and tanks are told to only use their AOE for aggro generation before switching to single target.

Industry observers note that it's all well and good trying to help players understand their role, but not when the information is outdated and fails to include key responsibilities. The tactical training exercises introduced early in Dawntrail are much better, and show how helpful such tutorials can be when they're properly updated and in line with over a decade's worth of in-game culture and community expectations.

Mollie spent her early childhood deeply invested in games like Killer Instinct, Toontown and Audition Online, which continue to form the pillars of her personality today. She joined PC Gamer in 2020 as a news writer and now lends her expertise to write a wealth of features, guides and reviews with a dash of chaos. She can often be found causing mischief in Final Fantasy 14, using those experiences to write neat things about her favourite MMO. When she's not staring at her bunny girl she can be found sweating out rhythm games, pretending to be good at fighting games or spending far too much money at her local arcade.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATE 17TH NOVEMBER: The Blood of Dawnwalker update 1.2 - the update that brings a Upcoming Game Plus mode, predominantly - is now available on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series S/X.

Industry observers note that upcoming Game Plus, as mentioned below, raises the level cap to 100, and scales enemies and regions in the game around you. Previously, the game was zone-scaled, so some zones were tougher than others. In New Game Plus, this will no longer be the case, so you can go and explore Xanthe's region at the back of Vale Sangora straight away, if you want to.

There'll be fresh versions of equipment with new stats to find, and they'll be labelled with "NG+" so you know when you've picked one up. You can unlock New Game Plus from the main menu after choosing your base save and difficulty option. All of your accrued skill perks and abilities will be available to you at the start of the Withering Away quest in the game's prologue.

The full patch notes for Dawnwalker revision 1.2 are:.

ORIGINAL STORY 13TH NOVEMBER: A New Game Plus mode is coming to vampiric RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker next week.

Developer Rebel Wolves has now detailed everything coming with The Blood of Dawnwalker's Revision 1.2, right now planned to go live sometime next week, and top of the list of changes is a New Game Plus for players who have already rolled credits on the game.

In a recent development, "If you completed the Epilogue, you can dive right back into Vale Sangora with Newly introduced Game+," the developer revealed earlier today. "Your level, skills, and inventory will carry over." Rebel Wolves is upping the level cap to 100 for New Game Plus, which will also have items with updated stats and enemies "balanced and scaled uniformly across all regions.".

Elsewhere in Update 1.2, the studio is making tweaks to "enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat," and improving terrain geometry to allow for "smoother movement during combat and exploration." We'll need to wait for more comprehensive patch notes before finding out which enemies are getting spongier or flimsier, however.

While the incoming patch doesn't seem to be as beefy as the last - the one that added animal petting and an easier Story mode - it'll be a good way to sink your teeth deeper into a game that's already begging to be replayed, thanks to a time management mechanic that can drastically change any given run.

It has been revealed that the new game from some former The Witcher 3 veterans came out in September and seems to have been a hit. Eurogamer's The Blood of Dawnwalker review called the game a "familiar dark fantasy adventure, but one with bold and provocative ideas of its own, that's mostly, enormously successful.".

#16722. Nearly a Decade Ago My Friend’s Private Plane Fell Out of the Sky. Then, in Florida This Month, It Happened to Another Friend.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1541 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vanityfair ↗ Open Full Page

Nearly a Decade Ago My Friend’s Private Plane Fell Out of the Sky. Then, in Florida This Month, It Happened to Another Friend.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I was in my late 20s, I lived in the worst building in the best part of SoHo.
  • The writer Deborah Schoeneman introduced me to her best friend from Cornell University, who she noted would be the perfect roommate.
  • Schoeneman, Grigoriadis, and Blumin in 2010 at Round Hill Resort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I was in my late 20s, I lived in the worst building in the best part of SoHo. My apartment above the French restaurant Raoul’s had been created by merging two units, so it was quite spacious. When I decided to move in with my boyfriend in Los Angeles, I still planned to spend a quarter of my time in New York and wasn’t about to give up this gem. But I figured I could find a roommate who would be psyched I wouldn’t be there a ton, and keep the smaller bedroom for myself.

The writer Deborah Schoeneman introduced me to her best friend from Cornell University, who she noted would be the perfect roommate. Jen Blumin was a Sex and the City character come to life: a tall, gorgeous blonde who managed a high-end event space with a private pool a few blocks away, mostly for corporate sponsors. I figured she wouldn’t be home much while I was, and told her if she had $1,800 a month, she had a deal. The day she moved in, she gingerly walked up the four flights of stairs carrying a large wrought-iron cage containing a shrieking bird. “Did I not tell you I had a cockatoo?” she asked with such insouciant camp, such mock innocence, that I just had to laugh.

Schoeneman, Grigoriadis, and Blumin in 2010 at Round Hill Resort.

Thus began one of my life’s great friendships, proceeding through many more ripostes, a decade of shared living space, and the birth of two kids each. Jen became wildly successful by turning vacant institutional buildings into heart-stopping event spaces, and even landed the contract for New York Fashion Week at the old post office across from Pennsylvania Station. The love of her life and father of her children, the architect James Ramsey, conceived of an idea with Dan Barasch, another Cornell chum, to create a “low line” under the old Delancy Street trolley terminal, and for a while it seemed like that was going to happen. But the relationship fell apart, and then things move very fast in my memory: Jen started to say she disliked New York City and wanted to live full time in the North Fork, a new boyfriend showed up, now she was moving to Puerto Rico for the climate and tax breaks, then she and the boyfriend were buying a private plane to fly direct from Puerto Rico to Islip, NY.

Sources indicate that when I heard about this fresh acquisition by my far-more successful friend, I have to admit I thought it sounded rad. Private planes occupy an almost mystical place in our culture. You’re up in the skies, free of seatmates chomping tuna sandwiches or annoyances like last-minute checked bags. You’re watching the clouds drift by, close enough to touch God. So what if her plane wasn’t the fanciest! It was still glamorous. As former Vanity Fair editor Tina Brown wrote on her Substack, everyone wants to be your friend when you have a plane: “The late TV legend Barbara Walters used to lament the necessity to vacation every year with the crass termagant CEO of a bra company just because remarked termagant happened to own her own plane.”.

According to recent reports, for the wealthy, private planes, which have become increasingly popular as a mode of transportation in recent years, aren’t only the ultimate in seclusion, but also the ultimate in spontaneity. You’re in a power position that’s completely the reverse of commercial flights, which reduce you to helpless nose-boned chattel. If you’re paying the bill, most decisions are controlled by you: You decide when you leave, who to invite, what to eat (certainly not pretzels and ginger ale), and whether there’s space for your three bulldogs.

It has been revealed that but the day after Mother’s Day in 2017—which Jen memorialized by sending a group text to myself and the core girlfriends with a snapshot of her two toddlers on a significant rock in Puerto Rico—Jen’s private plane fell out of the sky. She was flying with her children about 15 miles east of Eleuthera, an island in the Bahamas, in the Bermuda Triangle. None of them were found.

It has been revealed that I think a lot about Jen, but rarely more than now, nearly a decade after her death. That’s because this month, the same set of New York friends—loosely—are mourning another person who died with his family, including two more children under five years old. Adam Robinson, who chartered the Learjet that dove into a Florida road on November 1, leaving hypersurreal audio and video recordings that are now seared into the nation’s collective memory, arrived in New York a little later than Jen. I met him in the mid-2000s, but he seemed to be cut from the same cloth as she was: a tall, gregarious Lehman Brothers trader who had inherited a loft on lower Broadway from our mutual friends, the founders of the website College Humor (there was a lot of apartment swapping in lower Manhattan back then).

Adam was the definition of a “good guy”: smart, kind, and wry at the right moments. He had the open-hearted self-possession of someone who had traveled widely, but now he was in New York City to start his career, which, like so many of us, involved being hyper-social. He was not a close friend, but I was always happy to see him, and would usually spend 10 minutes at a crowded party chatting before moving on (this means a lot if you, like me, ascribe to the Fitzgeraldian notion that large parties provide intimacy, and prefer not to waste your breath in this rarefied milieu on dolts). A few guys in the crowd were into email marketing, and I heard that Adam had started a business in that industry but didn’t know much about his life after he moved to Austin, nor that he, too, had become quite successful.

It’s eerie that Adam’s private plane was headed to Eleuthra, the same area where Jen disappeared. But beyond that coincidence, what I keep returning to is how Jen and Adam’s stage in life had so many similarities: both in their 40s, too early to retire, they had nevertheless entered what you could call the “second phase” of success. They weren’t only trying to make money but to enjoy the money they’d made, and for them, that meant devising a new kind of life. Adam had moved from Austin to Aspen and wanted to pursue more outdoor adventures, some of which involved destinations hard to reach by commercial flights. Jen didn’t need to take her fatal private journey—JetBlue flies direct from San Juan to JFK—but having her own plane definitely came with bragging rights, though neither was the type to post a “flashing a peace sign on a PJ” semi-candid shot on Instagram.

And yet the private plane, so much a symbol of freedom and success for both Jen and Adam, led to their demise. This type of aviation is far less regulated than commercial planes, which hew to “strict government regulations enumerated in hundreds of pages of fine print…everything from the stowing of tray tables to announcements concerning lavatory smoke detectors,” as Jeff Wise wrote in Vanity Fair in 2025. That may be okay when you’re traveling in a $75 million G800, or as a guest of Drake in his $185 million plane, or with Kylie Jenner in her $73 million Bombardier, but when you’re on a small plane, it matters. Wise notes in his story that since 2020, almost half of the private plane crashes in the US have been Citations, which are on the smaller side.

And when traveling in a plane that lacks the sophistication of a commercial jet, whether you’re JFK Jr., Aaliyah, or just two people that everyone in a certain downtown Manhattan set knew in the mid-aughts, weather happens. Bad decisions in the cockpit compound, if the pilots even have time to make them. And then everything you’ve worked so hard for is lost, with the wreckage extending to family members and best friends left behind. “If I was Adam, I would rather be on the plane than on the ground” is the refrain I keep hearing from my friends this week, meaning that they’d rather perish with their families than live without them. Success and its luxuries are wonderful things. But they don’t guarantee you’ll get to come home.

#16721. Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1504 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games.
  • It has been revealed that unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95.
  • According to recent reports, microsoft, all the while, were taking notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

It has been revealed that unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

According to recent reports, microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a new physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming.".

For Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

On release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

Sources indicate that however, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

According to recent reports, the answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Consumers were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device.".

According to recent reports, in the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for customers. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

In a recent development, "I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he says. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

"The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find fresh uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat.".

When looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal users: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the issue of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

Industry observers note that all the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got big as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

Alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering customers.

"I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day.".

Rob Nelson, co-studio head of Rockstar North and GTA 6 lead, has explained that the game took so long simply because the studio had the option to.

Recent findings suggest that I don't think I'm surprising anyone by saying that GTA 6 has taken quite a while to come out. It's been 13 years, two console generations, and four Doctor Who actors since GTA 5, and it's made GTA 6 the most-anticipated game of all-time. And considering the first 10 GTA games were released in just 12 years, it kind of puts things into perspective just how long it's been, which feels even weirder when you realise we're just about a day away before people in New Zealand start playing it.

Speaking to The Guardian, Rockstar Games head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe adds that the devs "would never stop working on this game if they had the choice," with Nelson explaining, "it's really hard to close it down." He adds that with "a little bit of space from it, you can look at it objectively and go: 'I'm proud of what we've done.'" In the end, "it is being taken away from you.".

It has been revealed that nelson questions that if a developer had as many resources as Rockstar did, wouldn't they also go for the most ambitious game they could possibly make? He explains, "What we have grappled with is the transition from being limited by technical constraints to being limited by human resource constraints," adding, "You can keep going forever… People say you can throw money at the problem, and you can to an extent, but it's no guarantee of making something good.".

Recent findings suggest that kolbe adds, "They could have made GTA 5.5 and done it faster," but that “ultimately, that's not what they wanted." Nelson chimes in, "You have to take massive swings. It can't be just more of the same.".

In a recent development, sing Sing was one of my favorite movies of 2024 and one of the best movies of that year. Colman Domingo shines. He once again proves that he’s one of the best actors of his generation. Domingo’s brilliant scene partners, many not professionally trained actors, magnify his performance.

Using former Sing Sing Prison inmates, and some of those the story was based on, was a revolutionary idea. When I saw Union County, I became more convinced that films should enlist locals or real-life inspirations so those stories appear as characters in more films.

It has been revealed that will Poulter plays Cody, a man in a court-ordered recovery program in Union County. He’s doing fairly well in it until he reunites with his foster brother Jack (Noah Centineo). The film depicts both of their struggles to stay sober, while also highlighting these recovery programs and the people who use them. I first saw Union County at the Davis Theater in Chicago at a special screening with Poulter in attendance.

He explained his experiences with making the movie and having real people from Union County in it. You feel that community throughout. It, in a way, makes Union County feel more grounded in reality than other films with similar topics.

Addiction and recovery are popular subjects in art. Union County may be among the best films about addiction because it feels intimate and quiet while honestly and organically tackling addiction and recovery. Director Adam Meeks puts respect and care into the film’s authenticity and highlights the community without judgment.

Recent findings suggest that I love hearing filmmakers, actors, and creatives speak about their work. You get a better understanding of the process and intentions behind things. You also get a firsthand look at the passion for the project. Therefore, I enjoyed hearing Poulter speak about the importance Meeks and he put into their work with the community. Someone in the audience at the Davis Theater showing knew a person who appeared in the film. She therefore further highlighted how the community bonded even more while making Union County.

Many actors carry the prejudgment that they don’t like working or associating with those outside the acting and filmmaking world. Therefore, it is refreshing to see and hear about those who care about working with all scene partners, whether they’re an extra or an Oscar-winning actor, with the same courtesy, respect, and compassion.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Sources indicate that union County digs into the many aspects of addiction, including mental health. It’s another very honest movie about the mental struggles of addiction. Effectively showcasing things like the mental health struggles of addiction likely comes from consulting those with addiction while creating this film.

According to recent reports, besides Poulter and Centineo’s brilliant performances, Union County gets a lot of its power and authenticity from the people in the community playing extras or small roles. They don’t feel like people playing a part but those putting their real life on the screen in one way or another. It’s these types of lived experiences that make movies such as Sing Sing and Union County unique but also profound.

Recent findings suggest that many movies are all about escapism, while others remind you of the tragedy and hope of everyday life. The latter films often stay with you longer. It’s more transformative when those who understand the experience of the characters personally participate in the making of movies.

Netflix's long-gestating Magic: The Gathering animated series is called Planeswalker, and it's coming in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the title was revealed at MagicCon Atlanta, and Netflix shared a first look at the show on Twitter/X on 13th November. "Every great story begins with a spark. Here's your first look at Planeswalker, a latest animated series based on Magic: The Gathering. Coming to Netflix in 2027", the organization wrote, and shared a teaser, which you can see below:.

It has been revealed that according to a synopsis shared with IGN, the series follows Chandra Nalaar, "a volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past". It continues: "Confronted by an insidious force, Chandra and some of the most legendary Planeswalkers must harness their extraordinary abilities, navigate treacherous alliances, and battle their own inner demons to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence".

Netflix first revealed a Magic: The Gathering series in June 2019, with Avengers: Endgame directors Joe and Anthony Russo attached, and it was originally due in late 2022. Two years in, the original showrunners departed over creative differences, and in September 2024, Netflix confirmed it had started again from scratch with Star Trek: Picard and 12 Monkeys showrunner Terry Matalas in charge.

According to recent reports, IGN reports that Matalas, who most recently ran Marvel's VisionQuest, is running the show alongside Cindy Appel. Budapest-based studio DIGIC Pictures is handling the animation.

At the end of last month, we learned PUBG is also being turned into a live-action series for Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct, write, executive produce, and star.

Glover is a two-time Emmy and Golden Globe winner, best known for Atlanta and Community. Krafton calls PUBG "one of the world’s most enduring gaming franchises", and indicates the game, which is credited with popularising the battle royale genre, holds seven Guinness World Records.

Breaking: Judge denies motion to dismiss lawsuit accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of worsening RAM crisis by fixing memory prices and supply

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (343 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.
  • The class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year.
  • The trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a newly introduced motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

The class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

The trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a newly introduced motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

"But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.".

You know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which currently looks likely to last until at least 2028.
