📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What do you mean bad actors I wasn’t doing that much bad things pic.twitter.com/swHfeOLTuVNovember 16, 2026.

Sources indicate that bitly, the URL shortener website, got in hot water this week as users (or 'bad actors' as the firm calls them) found out they could hijack old broken links and put whatever they like in their place. As you can imagine, chaos ensued.

Many of the links have since been fixed, but it seems like the McDonald's Twitter account once accidentally mentioned the Swedish McDonald's team are responsible for 9/11,, and KFC linked to the Mewgenics wiki page for Steven, an NPC from the game. McDonald's was caught multiple times in this hijacking, with the Canadian X account hijacked to link the We Are Charlie Kirk song.

Though it's hard to verify now, it also seems like the Windows X page accidentally linked to the "r/FuckMicrosoft" subreddit too.

Industry observers note that major brands weren't the only ones caught in the mass hijacking. President Donald Trump seemingly tweeted a lot of Bitly links back in 2011, which were hijacked to instead link to a 'Trollface' meme song, a picture of a soggy cat titled "Soggy cat", and a link to the Epstein files Wikipedia page.

images for archival purposes pic.twitter.com/fRRr8LMGeENovember 15, 2026.

According to recent reports, A day after this exploit started to make its way around X, Bitly shared that it had identified the issue and remarked, "We have suspended the accounts involved and are disabling the affected links. Our Trust and Safety team is working to address the issue and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future.".

It has been revealed that it seems like the links in question were broken before being hijacked, and users simply managed to redirect those links to whatever site they wanted. However, in Bitly's documentation, it says the "back-halves used on these links cannot be re-used — whether they're automatically-generated or custom back-halves." So it's not entirely clear how these users manage to use links when Bitly says they supposedly cannot be reused.

Earlier today, we identified an matter that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts. We have suspended the accounts involved and are disabling the affected links. Our Trust and Safety team is working…November 15, 2026.

Sources indicate that in the grand scheme, brands linking to various songs and Wikipedia articles are relatively harmless, but the ability to hijack links does pose a problem: what if hackers could do the same with a link to something containing malware? As such, it's probably a good reminder to Bitly and any other URL shortener websites to double-check that customers can't reuse old broken links, as who knows who could have possibly made them first.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thursday is a massive day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially rolls out on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy upcoming Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance concerns: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Sources indicate that luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time rolls out tomorrow.

#16711. Scott Colom's Mississippi Is the One You Should Know

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2792 w)

Scott Colom's Mississippi Is the One You Should Know

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this is what an older Black woman remarked to MS NOW’s Nnamdi Egwuonwu as he interviewed Scott Colom supporters on the Tougaloo College campus Thursday night.
  • “To understand the world, you must first understand a place like Mississippi” is a more famous cautionary quip that scratches at the same sentiment.
  • According to recent reports, onlookers, including longtime national political strategists, seem surprised by Colom’s win.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Mississippi is not who you think we are.”.

Sources indicate that this is what an older Black woman remarked to MS NOW’s Nnamdi Egwuonwu as he interviewed Scott Colom supporters on the Tougaloo College campus Thursday night. The crowd was waiting for Colom to speak after his historic victory, becoming the first Black Mississippian elected to statewide office since Reconstruction, and its first Democratic senator in nearly a half century. The woman did not give her name, but her simple statement has tattooed itself inside my brain.

“To understand the world, you must first understand a place like Mississippi” is a more famous cautionary quip that scratches at the same sentiment. If you’ve known anyone from Mississippi, you’ve probably heard it. Everyone cites William Faulkner, even though nobody has definitively sourced it. But as the world looks with fresh eyes on my home state, the wisdom checks out.

According to recent reports, onlookers, including longtime national political strategists, seem surprised by Colom’s win. Mississippians are not. The extremes of the moral universe have always been duking it out down there, which makes Mississippi not strange or anomalous, but illustrative.

It has been revealed that there’s no avoiding the facts: Human beings have committed the most brutal violence imaginable against their fellow humans in Mississippi, as a matter of law and legacy. One of the consequences of that horror is that it has become prophecy. It is impossible not to feel a sense—from within the state and from without—of frustration and dread that it is taking way too long to emerge from a racism that has raptured the entire culture.

But to people who do not know Mississippians, who do not understand Mississippi—to those who suggest any right-minded or good people simply up and leave, or think the rest of the country should abandon all hope, or worse, look away entirely—you are missing one of the most notable threads in the future of American politics and culture. Colom got at this rub when he said that outlets like Cook Political Report, who prognosticate a “solid R” conclusion, are destructive. “They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long,” he wrote. And if you dismiss possibility in Mississippi, you are compounding the neglect. You are part of the destruction.

Mississippi is not who you think we are.

You think John McCain was a maverick? Scott Colom is a maverick.

In a recent development, during the race, he drew national attention not only for his prospect of flipping the unflippable, but also because he was doing so through one of the most vivid, creatively engaged, and original campaigns in modern politics. He built a coalition virally, with his twin brother, Andrew Robert Colom, as collaborator, offering “Sheeeeit” to the world (yes, that’s how many white Mississippians really talk), along with a Hollywood-worthy Sinners send-up, and Andrew’s searing spoken-word poem set to the strains of Fannie Lou Hamer. Colom even stood in line at a Trump rally to speak earnestly with voters who would otherwise be against him—I guarantee he won some of them over.

Industry observers note that his entire strategy was built on making people recognize Mississippi, in all its underdog idiosyncrasies. He asked Kamala Harris to campaign with him, even as his advisers reportedly told him it would be an error, because he knew she would draw media attention to underfunded hospitals. And he took the phone call informing him that he’d won while wearing a Richard Pryor hoodie. Because we like to laugh in Mississippi, okay?

As Kiese Laymon, novelist, memoirist, and modern-day Mississippi bard, told me, “Once I saw the protein ad, I knew he’d win.”.

History doesn’t echo in Mississippi; it rhymes. You can draw a straight line from the murders of Medgar Evers, or those of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, to the killings of Jorge Gomez or Renee Good or Alex Pretti. You can draw a straight line from Theodore Bilbo to Tate Reeves to Donald Trump.

As Kiese wrote in this magazine in 2020, Mississippi politics flow from its culture. (Incidentally, Kiese and Colom both attended Millsaps College, about 10 years apart, and had the same thesis adviser.) In “Mississippi: A Poem, in Days,” Kiese describes how he got into “an altercation with two fraternities on Bid Day”—when the students who want to be in the Greek system receive offers from frat and sorority houses. “Some fraternity members wore Confederate capes, Afro wigs, and others blackened their faces.” They called Kiese and his girlfriend the N-word.

Recent findings suggest that I have never written about the heartbreak of seeing the future governor of Mississippi in that group of white boys, proudly representing the Kappa Alpha fraternity and its confederate commitment to Black suffering. I have never admitted that after playing basketball against Tate all through high school, and knowing that he went to a public school called Florence, not a segregation academy, like so many other white boys we knew, it hurt my feelings to see Tate doing what white boys who pledged their identities to the Old South ideologies were supposed to do.

When I saw Tate in that confederate cacophony of drunken white boyhood, doing what they did, I knew he could one day be governor of Mississippi and president of the United States.

That is still the most damning thing I can ever say about a white boy from Mississippi.

It has been revealed that damning things still happen, and will again. Just days ago, as the votes continued to stack up for Colom, the old ugliness reared its head. White women in my hometown, students at the University of Mississippi, were captured on video making racist gestures—gesturing and making sounds like monkeys—at their Black neighbors’ video doorbell. The school, still embarrassingly insistent on calling itself “Ole Miss,” continues to investigate, while the offenders get so much more grace than they deserve from the victims and their families, as you can see in their CBS interview. I feel deep shame in these moments, because I know this is what so many people think Mississippi is. There is no excuse for it, and no explanation beyond the obvious. The shame should be obvious, too, but a white person from Mississippi is compelled to express it.

Recent findings suggest that the women are not from Mississippi, according to a source familiar; one, Alaina Kunes, is from Wisconsin, where a car dealership that bears her family’s name is now being sued for a separate allegation of racist actions. This is not an excuse, but rather a fear: that Mississippi’s reputation for the worst parts of history continues to attract the worst sorts of people.

But this is partly what Faulkner, or whoever it was, meant by understanding the world through the lens of Mississippi: Everywhere we must hope our better angels prevail.

I was born and raised in Mississippi among a large, politically engaged family who have wanted change for generations. When Sargent Shriver turned up unexpectedly at my grandparents’ house for dinner one night, on a swing through the South in a failed presidential bid, my grandmother whispered the urgent directive of “FHB”—“family holdback”—so her five sons would leave enough food for Shriver. This story, and that guest, was a point of pride her whole life. She was an unforgiving George McGovern campaigner; in our family photo album, among the pool parties and Christmas mornings, are pages of Polaroids she snapped of Richard Nixon’s televised resignation.

Sources indicate that local private schools, as I understood them, were inherently racist. Public school was a choice of one, and I got a world-class education in the Oxford school system. (Hyde-Smith attended Lawrence County Academy and she sent her own child to Brookhaven Academy, both segregation academies.) My class of 2000—I came up with the same kids from kindergarten through high school—was roughly half Black and half white, with the skinniest pie slivers of anything else. I left for college and never moved back, but my parents, brother, and extended family are still there. Today, Mississippi’s public-school students are doing better than most of their peers across the nation; my own children in the New York City school system are getting a more segregated, less excellent education than I did.

My father, a green-energy mayor and a Barack Obama appointee to the Tennessee Valley Authority (fired by Trump amid a Republican board takeover), pushed throughout my childhood to take the Confederate flag off the state flag and to remove the Confederate monument that still mars the Oxford Square. I was about eight years old when someone keyed “LIBERALS” into the trunk of our Honda Civic, probably because of the Ray Mabus for Governor bumper sticker. I recall being worried about it, until I saw that my parents were amused.

As white Southern liberals, we were in a tiny minority. And though the mantle was worn proudly, it was more existential than that—you were proud to be a Democrat not because it was one party over another, but because it was a stand-in for compassion, common good, and humanity. And nowhere could this be truer, or more necessary, than in Mississippi. (By way of disclosure, I see no conflicts in telling you all this. As former Time editor Rick Stengel states, “You should be non-partisan, but not neutral. Journalists must be biased in favor of the truth and facts. Biased in favor of democracy itself.” And this is the truth, in favor of democracy.).

Scott Colom and I were born a year apart in the earliest 1980s, during a sort of second-wave upcoming New South rebranding. More jobs were coming into the state thanks to manufacturing; more national attention was being paid to Black Mississippians’ cultural contributions (the Delta Blues Museum was established in 1979). William Winter was governor the years of our respective births, and he gave us free kindergarten. William Allain, whose moment was virtually destroyed by a racist, homophobic GOP slander campaign, followed. And Allain was succeeded by Mabus—who won on the slogan “Mississippi will never be last again.” Now, with the exception of Ronnie Musgrove, the governor has been a Republican since 1992. We’ve never had a Black person, or a woman for that matter. Have you had many good thoughts about Mississippi in all this time? I don’t think you have.

Heavy, Kiese’s devastating and raw memoir of coming of age as a Black boy in Mississippi, written in address to his activist and educator mother, gives his own view into 1980s and ’90s Mississippi: “You worked on Governor Mabus’s campaign and kept talking about how much was possible politically in Mississippi because it was the blackest state in the nation,” he writes. And his mother says to him: “Do you understand what’s possible if we actually get effective radical politicians in place down here?” Kiese responds, “I’m glad Mabus won but hearing about it every day is just kinda mee-guh.” Meager. It was not enough then, and we have plenty far to go.

Heavy was published in October 2018, just before Stacey Abrams turned Georgia purple, signaling to the rest of the country that it was time to take notice of the deeply disenfranchised Southern states.

Sources indicate that when I reached out to Mabus, who went on to become Bill Clinton’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia and then Obama’s Secretary of the Navy, he identified the dominoes that knocked toward Colom’s win: the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, rampant corruption, a welfare scandal featuring Brett Favre, and “office holders taking constituents for granted” over decades. Mabus was a young man working for Winter when Colom and I were little, and this election, he said, “brings hope for the future.”.

It doesn’t really matter which party you’d like to claim. Repulsive policies will eventually push everyone away. Mississippi Republicans are not moderate, are not descended of gentle governance. (See: Bilbo et al.) This is the state that put “personhood” on the ballot as part of a national antiabortion strategy; fortunately for all y’all, Mississippians rejected the idea of life beginning at conception. Lynn Fitch, the current attorney general, not only effortfully attempted to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, but she is the signed counsel for the petitioners in the Dobbs brief, which ultimately reversed Roe v. Wade. (Because I keep underscoring to you the infinite refractions of Mississippi, Fitch also went after Colom for one of his ads that used AI; he removed it.) Even the affidavit ballots that have taken so long to count are a result of strident, generational attempts by Republicans to disenfranchise Black voters. Which is why Mississippians knew, as the Colom–Hyde-Smith race came down to those affidavits, exactly in whose favor they would tally up. Were it not for the dedication of young Black canvassers—especially Black women—and homegrown mobilization efforts, things would have gone differently.

In a recent development, “There is a radical history of Black academics, activists, lawyers, and judges who have really been working to see a Mississippi where this was possible,” Kiese emailed me over the weekend. “I am thankful that someone like Leslie McLemore, who was a young member of Hamer’s Mississippi Democratic Party, can see what they worked and died for.”.

What does Colom’s win mean for Kiese? “It means that the people, not any party, get what they organize and fight for,” he replied. “Our state taught the world that again last week.”.

Industry observers note that my privileged position occluded my own understanding of Mississippi’s true potential until I was older. Growing up, I mostly just clocked defeat—every presidential election, every midterm, Mississippi was red as red could be, as Mississippi’s poverty levels ratcheted toward a 21st-century high of 24%. In 2008, John McCain beat Barack Obama in the state by a 13% margin (the two staged a debate in Oxford). In 2016, Trump bested Hillary Clinton by almost 18 points.

According to recent reports, after Trump won in 2024, an old childhood friend who’d gone MAGA texted me a GIF of a penis ejaculating stars that reconstituted in the shape of a patriotic eagle. Flash forward a year later, he’s angry about gas prices, and, more striking to me, horrified by the war in Gaza. Colom’s protein ad is for him, and that nerve of enthusiasm it struck is going to keep firing.

According to recent reports, colom didn’t run on pronouns or any numerical strain of woke. He has remarked he is a fan of Trump’s border security, agrees with him on certain tax policies, and supports the Second Amendment. When asked about improving wages for government employees, he has said he wants to take care of teachers—and cops. As Colom told Jen Psaki in a televised interview, “We gotta be a party that represents our whole country, that understands all parts of the country.”.

Recent findings suggest that now that people outside Mississippi are waking up to Colom, leftists may find his centrism irritating or even offensive. You may find a new reason to look down your noses at Mississippi. It all but promises to provide an opportunity.

So I will just leave you with the brothers Colom.

Industry observers note that “They lied about Mississippi. Stated that evil lived in one state, but the cotton cow fed the nation. Europe eating off the same plate. They lied about Mississippi. Said the torture was only here, but the banker’s desk in northern mills still dripping blood from hostage tears. They lied to us all. That’s propaganda machine on both sides, running on slander…. Denying the nation condoned it, denying the nation owned it, denying the nation fed off pain…. They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state.”.

He claims, invoking Hamer, “Mississippi Freedom Party began again.”.

And the vision of Scott: “There is nothing wrong with Mississippi that can’t be fixed by what’s right.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Call of Duty Endowment is marking Remembrance Day and its 17th anniversary by encouraging Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone players to pick up its Valor Pack, with all of Activision's net proceeds going towards helping veterans find jobs.

The Call of Duty Endowment Valor Pack - which has been available since Modern Warfare 4 released on 23rd October - was designed by the Endowment and Infinity Ward with US Marine Corps veteran and Medal of Honor recipient Kyle Carpenter in mind.

The items include a melee weapon blueprint inscribed with "Worth Fighting For", plus items called Relentless and Still Standing.

According to the Call of Duty blog, 100 percent of Activision's net proceeds from the pack (after VAT and sales tax) go to the Endowment.

To mark Remembrance Day, players who owned it and debuted either game before 6pm GMT on 12th November also received double XP tokens and a DMZ survival kit.

"Veterans bring incredible skills into the workplace after military service," stated Carpenter.

The Endowment, which supports veterans in the UK as well as the US, states it has now helped place more than 180,000 into "high-quality jobs", and wants to reach 200,000 by 2030.

Other partners are also raising money, with Pilot's round-up campaign raising more than £4.7 million ($6 million) for the Endowment since 2019. Polaris will also donate around £19,500 ($25,000) if players collectively complete 5 million rides in its DAGOR vehicle across Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone by 25th November.

Sources indicate that it comes two weeks after Activision apologised to bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it would remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Players discovered that the game's opening cinematic uses short news clips to depict fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. Those clips have since been found to include archive footage from the 2022 Itaewon disaster, in which around 160 people died.

Call of Duty's anti-cheat team Ricochet recently announced it's officially cracking down on Warzone Agent.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic.
  • This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on.
  • Sources indicate that as for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star.

Recent findings suggest that split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

Sources indicate that as for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an issue for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming enhancement, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Batman 2 has taken so long to make that Robert Pattinson is reportedly no longer legally contracted to appear in a third movie, leaving the future of DC Elseworlds' Caped Crusader unclear.

Recent findings suggest that according to a latest report from The Wrap, "the protracted production of The Batman: Part II has allowed Pattinson to slip out from under his contract." The deal originally held the star to make a third and final outing as the Gotham vigilante. But now that the contract will have seemingly timed out by the time of a third movie, it is not clear what will happen to Pattinson's Bat.

The Batman sequel has seen its fair share of setbacks. Originally set to release in October 2025, it was pushed back multiple times all the way to early 2028. Most recently, the project was momentarily put on hold when director Matt Reeves stepped away from production for personal reasons. However, filmmaker Steven Soderbergh has now taken the reins. Still, The Batman: Part II is certainly a long time coming, as the first movie hit screens in 2022 – six years before the sequel is set to release.

Pattinson's recent casting as a legendary agent 007 further complicates things. On November 16, it was announced that Pattinson had been cast as the next James Bond, in Amazon MGM Studios' first take on the British spy led by Dune director Denis Villeneuve. Despite Pattinson previously stating he would only sign on to three Bond movies and being a few years older than the other candidates, he still landed the role.

It has been revealed that james Bond movies are a huge undertaking, which will certainly take up a lot of Pattinson's time moving forward, leaving little room for The Batman. Alas, Pattinson has proven he can take on big projects one after the other. Just this year, Pattinson has starred in The Drama, The Odyssey, Primetime, and will be introduced to the world of Dune this December in Villeneuve's third and final movie.

Industry observers note that there is also the issue of DC Studios. Just last week, it was confirmed that James Gunn and Peter Safran would be stepping down as DC Studios co-CEOs, and are set to be replaced by former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham on December 1, 2026. The shakeup arrived not long after Skydance-owned Paramount acquired Warner Bros. Reports suggest that Skydance looks to "dismantle" Gunn's DCU Chapter One.

In a recent development, though The Batman isn't part of the DCU, the fate of all current DC projects remains ambiguous. DC Studios, Pattinson, and Reeves have yet to comment on the matter.

In a recent development, the Batman 2 is set to hit theaters on February 18, 2028. For more, check out our guide on how to watch the DC movies in order and keep up with other upcoming DC movies and demonstrates.

I previously worked in communications after graduating with an MA in journalism. In my spare time, you can find me binging horror movies or getting lost in a cosy little game on my Switch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that YES! There are spoilers below for You Can See Everything, which you can still catch in theaters as part of the 2026 movie schedule.

According to recent reports, now that the cat is officially out of the bag regarding Amanda Seyfried’s surprise role in the hit A24 release You Can See Everything, I’ve been waiting to hear from Christopher Abbott. The East of Eden star plays Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, in the recreations that Seyfried is also a part of. Like so many spoilers in the movie, the cast and crew have been pretty mum about the production. Finally, we’ve heard from Abbott.

According to recent reports, abbott has been very busy over the last couple of years with projects like Wolf Man and The Testament of Ann Lee, plus his Tony-nominated performance in Death of a Salesman on Broadway this year. He's been a little overshadowed in the hype around You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Seyfried’s appearance is such a WTF moment that, speaking as an audience member, it’s almost like we were all still processing that to even register Abbott’s cameo as Evans. It took a couple of minutes before I put it together, honestly. Abbott himself admitted to the process being rushed for him, as well, telling The Hollywood Reporter:.

Nathan and Lance, not that long before I went to go work on [it], had just called me and asked me to come mess around. I got to see some of the footage that they had shot before. I did it, so you know, it was a very kind of quick run-and-gun thing for me, at least.

Abbott also revealed that because it was so quick, he didn’t have a lot of time to prepare or study the character and relied on the footage that Fielder and Oppenheim shot while they were embedded with Holmes and Evans before the former Theranos fraudster reported to prison in 2023. Of the prep, Abbott says:.

I've been a fan of both of them for a long time, so I kind of remarked yes before they even told me what they wanted to do. For me, it was just sort of fun to not to make it so basic. I didn't really know of him until they highlighted me the footage from the thing. So I just thought it was a very interesting character. I didn't dive deep. I sort of had just enough time to maybe try to do some version of mimicry or find little nuances. He's an interesting subject.

It has been revealed that I think part of what makes it work so well in the box office hit is that we, as an audience, like Abbott, weren’t really familiar with Evans. By the time Abbott appears, we know as much about Evans as he did when he took the role. He’s playing the same villainous character we’ve seen over the previous two hours of the movie, and it works really well.

It has been revealed that abbott probably won’t get any Oscar buzz like Seyfried is getting, but that’s not a slight on him in the least. He provides another bonkers moment in a movie full of them. I really can’t wait for this movie to hit streaming so I can really dive back into it and his performance.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to Insider Gaming, the project is in early development at Ubisoft Montreal under the codename Spades.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubisoft is reportedly working on a upcoming Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

According to Insider Gaming, the project is in early development at Ubisoft Montreal under the codename Spades. It’s one of three newly introduced projects reportedly in production at the studio, and sources suggest a second of those is also set in the Rainbow Six universe. Eurogamer hasn’t been able to verify the report.

According to recent reports, it’s not yet clear what form the new game will take, but Insider Gaming’s sources mentioned it's "likely Vegas 3 rather than a remake" of an existing game. Insider Gaming expects it will be several years before Ubisoft officially confirms a new Vegas game.

Rainbow Six Vegas launched in 2006, followed by Rainbow Six Vegas 2 in 2008. Since then, the series has centred on 2015's Rainbow Six Siege, and in August, Ubisoft unveiled Rainbow Six Tactics, a single-player, turn-based spin-off from Ubisoft Paris due in 2027.

Rainbow Six now sits under Vantage Studios, the Ubisoft subsidiary set up last year that also oversees Assassin’s Creed and Far Cry, and in which Tencent holds a 26.32 percent stake.

Sources indicate that last week, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on two new Assassin's Creed games: one set in ancient Rome, and a mobile spin-off set in Jerusalem. The leak came less than a week after Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, insisting there are presently no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

Recent findings suggest that I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier.

According to recent reports, look, I'll be real with you. When I installed Drag Meets – Quick n Dirty Edition, I was not expecting it to go well. Cars spend most of their time flying and exploding in my copy of Grand Theft Auto 5, and these circumstances aren't conducive to gentlemanly racing.

I didn't anticipate it going quite as badly as it did, though. Drag Meets is actually rather complex: you don't just rock up to an objective marker, tap E, and get warped behind the wheel of a car. There's a lite social sim element to the whole thing, so you walk up to an objective marker, tap E, and suddenly find yourself standing in the midst of a drag racing soirée.

Drag meets are a scene, it turns out, and the scene's members have names, goals, and ambitions. A racer named "Blue Anime Panto" is seeking a challenger, the notifications inform me. "Blade had joined the meet", reads another. A lady called Tempesta has been forced to leave the meet because her engine broke, apparently. How did this happen? Either it's a randomly rolled event or her car flew into the sun; I am unable to tell.

It's not just Tempesta who's leaving the meet. Everyone is leaving, on account of the airborne minivan, just overhead, filled with hitmen determined to kill us all. They should be determined to kill me and only me, but Lamar (from GTA 5, you know? Lamar was also there. Keep up) began shooting back at them and all hell broke loose.

The drag race—if it's even possible—never got the opportunity to start. Pretty soon, racing legends like Stinger GT and Rhapsody were face-down in the Los Santos grass. And then I teleported to the airport.

Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game.
  • Industry observers note that the difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth.
  • Industry observers note that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

Industry observers note that the difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

Industry observers note that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

It makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

It has been revealed that thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

It's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

In terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock new rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make new, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

  • Recent findings suggest that it's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together.
  • A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that what if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

Recent findings suggest that it's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that this one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

Recent findings suggest that when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

In a recent development, based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate promptly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very promptly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

In a recent development, we are now just four days away from the release of GTA 6 on Xbox Series X/S and PS5, but the proximity to the much-anticipated launch date isn't stemming the tide of leaks that has been plaguing the game for much of the past year. Yesterday, a newly introduced video - seemingly from a record store that received vinyl records of the soundtrack early - indicated off the full 34-song tracklist for the game.

Thanks to the listing printed on the back of Grand Theft Auto 6: The Album vinyl, we have a better idea of the licensed music that'll appear in-game. Travis Scott, Rina Sawayama, Cardi B, Pinkpantheress, SZA, Keith Richards, Dua Lipa, Jennie, Lana Del Rey, Zara Larsson are just some of the names that make up the impressive list. We know about a few of these tracks from September's announcement of the record, but only six tracks were revealed then, not the whole list.

Take a look at the full track listing below:.

You can expect to hear these tracks on the radio - alongside many more, no doubt - and deployed at curated times during cutscenes or in missions, to really tie together the vibe of the city. This is something Vice City did remarkably well its roster of 80s tracks, and I can't wait to see how Rockstar has used more contemporary music in the same way here.

In a recent development, of course, there have been a lot of Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks in the run-up to the game's launch. Another recent example is the full game's map which seemingly leaked online thanks to the £350 collector's edition on show in a UK department store. Then there were all the leaks from a group calling itself CyberLeek, which shared unofficial gameplay and map details over the course of a few weeks, before Rockstar had even revealed much gameplay itself.

Amongst all this, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Makes a Weak Case for His Post-Trial Comeback

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for weeks, Los Angeles has been plastered with posters of a malevolent-looking man in a top hat and gray sideburns.
  • “It’s good to be back,” Depp gurgles in the movie’s trailer.
  • I adored Johnny Depp back in his Edward Scissorhands/Gilbert Grape/Ed Wood heyday; he probably would’ve been my hall pass if I’d known about the concept back then.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for weeks, Los Angeles has been plastered with posters of a malevolent-looking man in a top hat and gray sideburns. It always takes me a few minutes to process that this elderly curmudgeon is Johnny Depp, doing his Hollywood walk of shame in Ebenezer.

“It’s good to be back,” Depp gurgles in the movie’s trailer. He’s either reveling in his return from infamy or trolling the audience, depending on your point of view.

I adored Johnny Depp back in his Edward Scissorhands/Gilbert Grape/Ed Wood heyday; he probably would’ve been my hall pass if I’d known about the concept back then. Now, though, it feels as if the once chiseled-cheeked heartthrob has found a character that suits him: a monstrous figure seeking redemption.

In a recent development, “Grant me the grace to prove that I am no longer the man that I once was,” Ebenezer Scrooge begs one of the ghosts haunting him in this rather plodding latest version of Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol, directed by horror auteur Ti West. Scrooge is trying to make up for a lifetime of stinginess and cruelty, whereas Depp seeks to win back mainstream audiences after the ugly, drawn-out brawl that was his marriage and divorce from Amber Heard.

Heard alleged that he was an abusive addict. Depp denied abusing her and filed two defamation suits. He aimed one at the British tabloid The Sun for calling him a wife-beater (which he lost, since the court found the characterization to be “substantially true”). The other was leveled at Heard for describing herself in a Washington Post op-ed as “a public figure representing domestic abuse.” What started as a defamation trial ended up as a livestreamed referendum on post-#MeToo gender politics.

Industry observers note that the saga spawned organized smear campaigns soaked in misogyny. Social media erupted with vile memes, hashtags, and videos targeting Heard, bearing hashtags like #AmberHeardIsAPsychopath and #DontBelieveAllWomen. One men’s group debuted a “Ditch the Witch” protest in support of Depp. It seemed to echo one of Depp’s texts about Heard, released during the trial, in which he proposed to a friend: “Let’s drown her before we burn her!!!…I will fuck her burnt corpse afterwards to make sure she is dead.” And it wasn’t just ordinary guys taking up arms for Depp. Moments after the verdict was unveiled, the GOP’s House Judiciary tweeted a GIF of Depp in Pirates of the Caribbean from its official account, showing support for him.

“The craziness [aimed at Heard] was a kind of pent-up anger at women,” a film producer suggested to me back in 2022. “I think it really stirred up a lot of deep-seated resentment that hasn’t been allowed expression since #MeToo.”.

Depp didn’t come out of the crucible with his career intact. He was asked to resign from the Fantastic Beasts franchise—though Warner Bros. still paid Depp his full $16 million salary—and his former agent claimed Disney dropped him from the next Pirates of the Caribbean movie. Still, he never really went away. In fact, like so many guys who have been supposedly “canceled,” he wormed his way back in quite easily. In 2023, he got a standing ovation at Cannes for his role as Louis XV in the French film Jeanne du Barry. The next year, he directed the movie Modì, Three Days on the Wing of Madness. Meanwhile, producer Jerry Bruckheimer confirmed in 2025 that he’s been talking to Depp about a sixth Pirates film after all. All the while, Depp has also kept his massive brand deal as the face of Dior’s Sauvage.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t feel boycotted by Hollywood because I don’t think about Hollywood,” Depp revealed imperiously a few years back. “I don’t have much further need for Hollywood.” Enter Ebenezer, his official return to…Hollywood. Which he doesn’t need or think about. At all.

Call it Christmas-washing: What could be more wholesome and uncontroversial than A Christmas Carol? According to Variety, Paramount paid Depp just $5 million—a big drop-off from the days when he could reportedly command $50 million for a single film—and only spent $38 million to produce the movie, hedging its bets. Still, this film is a pretty warm welcome back to American movie screens, major marketing campaign and all.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, Depp’s mediocre performance in Ebenezer doesn’t dispel the sour scent of desperation that hangs over his career. Scrooge is one of the most unlovable characters in all of literature, and Depp’s charm does not shine through the gnarled facial prosthetics. He plays the archetypal miser in the broadest of ways, spending much of the nearly two-hour movie alternating between exaggerated expressions of cantankerousness and horror. Depp’s inspiration for the role might as well have been Oscar the Grouch, though one with less educational value who’s hollow at his core. At various points, the actor campily throws himself into physical comedy that is at odds with the horror-soaked vibe of West’s production.

Knowing this is a test run for Depp’s uncanceling, viewers will find it hard not to see Ebenezer as a wink-filled plea for absolution. “I’m not the man I was!” his character screams over and over. “Allow me my redemption.” To which the answer—or my answer, at least—is simple: Bah, humbug.

Tech Report: Robert Pattinson is the perfect choice for 007's new era, and his casting reveals what we can expect from Bond 26

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamesradar

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A decade ago, Robert Pattinson seemed absolutely done with franchises.
  • How times have changed; not only is Pattinson Batman, but now he's James Bond, too.
  • It has been revealed that pattinson first gave us a glimpse of his Bond-ness in David Cronenberg’s Cosmopolis, playing a cold-faced billionaire with a penchant for a tight black suit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A decade ago, Robert Pattinson seemed absolutely done with franchises. He was still, to most people, either Edward Cullen or Cedric Diggory – a teen heartthrob whose every movement was stalked. "I had people sitting outside my house every single day, and it drove me crazy,” he told NME back in 2015. "I didn't go into a supermarket for about six years.".

How times have changed; not only is Pattinson Batman, but now he's James Bond, too. It's a casting that, two weeks ago, nobody could have seen coming, and yet, despite the years of rumors about Henry Cavill, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, and Callum Turner, Pattinson’s last-minute swoop to take on 007 feels inevitable, the culmination of an incredibly varied and interesting career that's only grown in stature.

It has been revealed that pattinson first gave us a glimpse of his Bond-ness in David Cronenberg’s Cosmopolis, playing a cold-faced billionaire with a penchant for a tight black suit. It was severely underseen – thanks, in part, to coming out the same year as the final Twilight instalment – but it gave Pattinson a taste for something beyond romance and vampires, and his interests rapidly shifted to quirky, complex characters in arthouse projects from up-and-coming directors.

In Good Time, he played a wounded bank robber with deep-rooted brotherly concerns; in High Life, he was a criminal sent to space; in The Lighthouse, an isolated lighthouse keeper who goes insane after spending a few weeks with Willem Dafoe. Each film gave Pattinson space to grow onscreen, showcasing his sheer talent as an actor – fueled perhaps by a desire to prove himself more than just Edward Cullen (even immediately after the announcement, articles were being written about how Pattinson will never outgrow the role).

Come the 2020s, Pattinson was back in blockbusters. First, there was Tenet, bringing him into Christopher Nolan's orbit and giving Pattinson a true Bond audition (lest we forget how much Nolan loves Bond; he told us as much a few times). Pattinson played Neil, a sharp-shooting, charming agent who helps John David Washington's CIA operative navigate the time-twisting narrative. Then, two years later, Pattinson was a moody, emo incarnation of The Batman, a role many couldn't see him filling out, yet the movie is now heralded as one of the best Batman flicks, up there with Nolan's own Dark Knight.

Recent findings suggest that this year, Pattinson has felt almost omnipresent, thanks to back-to-back-to-back parts in The Drama, The Odyssey, Primetime, and, coming soon, Dune 3. If you’ve been to a cinema over the last 12 months, you've almost certainly seen at least one Pattinson show, and if you've seen them all, you've witnessed his sheer range (and his array of accents).

Pattinson’s last-minute swoop to take on 007 feels inevitable, the culmination of an incredibly varied and interesting career that’s only grown in stature.

So, to recap, we know Pattinson can wear a suit well, is good with a gun, and can play characters in a variety of deeply complicated emotional states – plus, lest we forget, he remains a heartthrob – all of which point to someone more than capable of, if not perfect for, playing Bond. But beyond that. Pattinson's casting also states a lot about what might be different about incoming director Denis Villeneuve’s vision for MI6's finest.

Pattinson has thrived playing characters with a certain darkness; he has the raw charisma to be Chris Hansen in Primetime, but, at the same time, can inhabit those shades of black that give a character like him real life. The same can be noted about Pattinson's part in Good Time (still my favorite movie of his), in which he makes us care deeply for such a terrible person.

It has been revealed that daniel Craig's version of Bond had similar complexities: he was a mature Bond who could be charming, but who also felt immense guilt and had so much internal strife. Frankly, I was sure Amazon would push Bond to be a little more lighthearted post-Craig, harkening back to the Roger Moore and Pierce Brosnan days, but Pattinson's casting hints at continuing down the more serious Craig route. No doubt, he will still be a womanising, martini-drinking killer, but we're also living in a modern world that's going to shit, with the computers taking over, and maybe we need a Bond who feels very human, with all the fallibilities of a man.

Indeed, Pattinson brings a certain broodiness, vulnerability, and unpredictability that feels just right for the times. Think now of Pattinson in The Odyssey: could anyone else have delivered the line "Get these beggars out of here" with such weird gusto? Now imagine that sort of delivery brought to Bond. It's not what you expect, but it's wildly watchable.

It's also worth noting Pattinson's age. At 40, he's the oldest name recently bandied about as auditioning for Bond – everyone else was in their early-to-late 30s, and even Henry Cavill was believed to be too old for the role at the ripe age of 43. Bond needs to be a little older to have the scars of a life well lived, and Pattinson's age confirms this isn't going to be the young Bond idea once pitched by Tom Holland. On the business side, Pattinson also makes a lot of sense. This year's Primetime saw its box office driven mainly by Gen Z, with 69 per cent of turnout from under-30s, and with a new Bond having to win over a new generation, Pattinson has already shown he can do exactly that.

Who were the other Bond candidates? A recap of the race to become the next James Bond.

Recent findings suggest that yet, there's also one huge negative that comes with Bond being played by someone who's already a box office draw: people have expectations. I mean, I've speculated about what Pattinson’s Bond could look like right here in this piece!

Industry observers note that really, though, my hope – and what we should all expect – is for Pattinson to do something completely different from anything he's done before, and from anything we've ever seen from Bond before. That's what makes him an extremely exciting choice, because wherever Villeneuve takes Bond next, we know Pattinson has the talent to pull off the role and, most importantly, make it unique to him.

According to recent reports, I just fear that, like back in those Twilight days, he may not be able to go into a supermarket again without being gawped at. That’s just the price you pay to say those immortal words on screen: the name's Bond… James Bond.

Bond 26 does not at the moment have a release date. For more, here's our ranking of the best Bond movies.

Recent findings suggest that unity's next venture, amidst rumours of it being bought out by the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, is the Unity Fellowship, a grant program that offers $50k in cash to Unity-using indie devs that plan release a game within a year - without asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or IP ownership in exchange. I don't need to tell you that all sounds too good to be true, even with the Unity engine requirement, but in fairness, the manufacturer has form for handing out cash. The Unity for Humanity grant, just earlier this year, spread $600K across ten different indie projects focused on societal and environmental issues.

Unity states that ten recipient studios will receive the Fellowship's cash grant, as well as direct partnership with Unity staff, industry connections, spots at Unity events and PR/marketing support. Even studios with an existing publisher can apply, if they think that "the Fellowship could still make a real difference for your game." It also clarifies that their policy regarding AI use is that "We don't require you to list the tools you used, but you must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content", which doesn't come as a huge surprise considering Unity's excitement around its Unity Spark game-generating AI tool.

It has been revealed that the grant is also not open to "countries or regions subject to U.S. sanctions", such as Russia, Iran and Cuba, as well as Brazil, Italy and Quebec due to "local regulations." For developers not in those areas, applications for the grant are open until December 18th, with the recipients to be notified by the end of February 2027. If you're a developer who's interested, you can apply here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that blade Runner 2099 - an upcoming TV miniseries coming to Amazon Prime Video, acting as a sequel to Blade Runner (1982) and Blade Runner 2049 (2017) - might be getting a video game. And a 'triple-A' video game, at that. At least that's according to Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, executive producers for Blade Runner 2099 and co-CEOs of Alcon Entertainment (which owns the Blade Runner IP).

It has been revealed that in a new interview with IGN, the duo reveal that they had thought about adapting the Blade Runner fracnhise into a game, and that - should it come to fruition - it would target "triple-A" in scope. Other than that, the duo seemed to want to keep any potential information to themselves. Given they appear to be in talks about the title, rather than in any active development, if something did come of this ideation, it would no doubt be a long, long way off. Kosove and Johnson's aim seems to be getting players to "interact" more with the world of Blade Runner, which has recently been fleshed out by the 2017 movie and is set to be developed more in the upcoming series.

Of course, we've seen Blade Runner games before. There was 1997's simply-titled Blade Runner - developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Interactive - which was a point-and-click adventure that really seemed to pick up the vibes the original Ridley Scott was putting down. An Enhanced Edition of the game was released in 2022, which is actually more of a remake than a simple enhancement.

Industry observers note that then, in 2023, Annapurna Interactive unveiled its very first internally-developed game, in the form of Blade Runner 2033: Labyrinth. The game, which promised to riff on the dystopian universe established in Ridley Scott's cult classic movie, would have been sandwiched squarely between that film and its sequel, Blade Runner 2049. It was going to be set in LA after the Blackout hits, but beyond that - and the fact it's coming to PC and consoles at some point - few details ever managed to break through the PR barrier before the game went dark: it's been removed from Annapurna's website and delisted from Steam. Curious.

If you want to see something more from the cyberpunk world sooner, Blade Runner 2099 releases on Prime Video on 25th November.

According to recent reports, for many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for crucial pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this newly introduced Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

It has been revealed that this is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

Industry observers note that if you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a fresh tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an notable document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world has been waiting with bated breath for the announcement of who will be the next actor to take on the role of James Bond. The rumors have been swirling for months over who would take on the role in the upcoming Denis Villeneuve-directed Bond flick. They've really heated up in the last few weeks as auditions and screen tests have been underway for the upcoming 26th installment of the Bond franchise. Now we know, and it turns out it’s one of the biggest names in Hollywood: Robert Pattinson.

In a recent development, I’m actually a little shocked by this cast, but I’m not mad about it. I was leaning into the Jack Lowden or Callum Turner casting rumors, because I actually didn’t think it would be a star as big as Pattinson stepping into the shoes of the eight men who have previously played Bond. Pattinson has a huge year on the 2026 movie schedule, and this ensures the next couple of years will be busy too, after the announcement was made on social media this morning.

Sources indicate that of course, Pattinson is no stranger to iconic roles. Filming is (hopefully) coming to a close soon on The Batman Part II, in which Pattinson is reprising his role as the Caped Crusader in the second installment of the Matt Reeves Batman franchise. Production on that film has been a slow go, with Reeves recently stepping aside temporarily and Steven Soderbergh joining to finish the principal photography.

Recent findings suggest that major franchises are also nothing upcoming for Pattinson. Not only did he have his breakout in the Twilight franchise, but he's also joined the cast of Dune: Part III, which is coming to theaters in about a month on what many are calling "DunesDay," as it coincides with the release of Avengers: Doomsday. It is the culmination of the Dune trilogy, also directed by Villeneuve. It certainly bodes well for the next Bond movie that the two clearly have a good working relationship.

I do think the choice of Pattinson to play 007 will come with some controversy, but that’s to be expected. There was never a chance that Amazon/MGM, who own the Bond franchise now, were going to avoid it, no matter who they chose. Pattinson is probably the biggest star to ever be cast in the role for the first time, rivaling when Pierce Brosnan got the role way back in 1994 before GoldenEye. The fact that he is such a massive star has caused some blowback, but I think it was to be expected now that Amazon controls the franchise. They are going to invest a lot of money in this. A safe choice of a big star was probably inevitable.

Sources indicate that there is still a lot to learn about Bond 26, like who will be the next "Bond Girl" and the rest of the characters we all love, like M and Q. We’ll be busy keeping you updated on all the developments.

See Bruce Springsteen, Martin Scorsese, and Surprise Guest Tom Cruise Honor Steven Spielberg at MoMA
